criteria.descriptor: Full marks: the governance mechanisms are technically sound — authorization enforced at the tool boundary rather than in the prompt, a scoped least-privilege/on-behalf-of identity, approval tiers correctly keyed to reversibility/blast radius, an accurate characterization of prompt-injection/confused-deputy risk (lethal trifecta), and valid audit/attribution fields. Deduct for asserting prompt-based controls suffice, treating the model as a trust boundary, or misdescribing the injection mechanism.

Full marks: addresses all four required areas — permission/identity model, risk-tiered HITL gating, the injection threat model with containment, and audit/attribution plus runtime controls (budgets, circuit breaker, kill switch, staged rollout) — and notes registry governance. Partial credit scales with how many of these are substantively covered rather than named in passing.

Full marks: justifies design choices through the autonomy/velocity vs. blast-radius/reversibility trade-off, explains why prompt-level controls are insufficient, and ties gate strictness and rollout caution to action risk and accumulated eval evidence. Weak answers list controls without explaining why or when each applies.

Full marks: organized as a coherent framework a review board could act on, using precise terminology (least privilege, blast radius, dry-run/plan, on-behalf-of identity, audit trail, kill switch, canary/shadow) correctly. Deduct for disorganized or vague prose that blurs the distinct controls.

expected_answer_points: Enforce authorization at the tool boundary, not via prompt instructions — the model is not a trust boundary and can be jailbroken/injected, so 'telling the model not to' is insufficient
Least-privilege, scoped dedicated agent identity (not a human's broad credentials/super-token); per-tool RBAC and read/write separation; on-behalf-of identity intersecting agent and user permissions

Risk-tiered human-in-the-loop approval keyed to reversibility/blast radius (auto for read-only; gate irreversible/high-blast actions like Terraform apply, prod merge, pod restart), with plan/dry-run before applying

Prompt-injection / confused-deputy threat model: untrusted tool outputs and retrieved content can drive privileged actions (the 'lethal trifecta' of sensitive access + untrusted content + consequential action); contain via allowlists, provenance tagging, argument constraints
Action budgets, rate limits, loop/runaway detection, and circuit breakers plus global/per-tool kill switches
Immutable structured audit trail per tool call: triggering user, tool + args + result, prompt/registry version, model+version, trace id — sufficient for attribution, reconstruction and rollback
Staged rollout gated by evaluation and adversarial red-teaming: shadow, then canary with write tools disabled, enabling privileged tools only after injection testing; rollback plan

Governance of the shared tool/prompt registry itself (review, ownership, versioning, re-evaluation on change) since adding a tool expands the agent's capability surface; and explicit articulation of the autonomy-vs-blast-radius trade-off
common_pitfalls: Relying on the system prompt to enforce permissions (e.g. 'instruct the model never to run Terraform in prod') instead of enforcing authorization at the tool boundary — the model can be injected or jailbroken and is not a trust boundary

Treating prompt injection as only an output-safety/content-filtering problem, missing that untrusted tool outputs and retrieved rows can drive privileged tool calls (confused deputy / lethal trifecta)
Giving the agent a human's broad credentials or one super-token, so blast radius equals everything, with no scoped identity or per-tool least privilege
Applying human approval uniformly to every action (destroying the velocity the project exists for) or auto-approving everything (unsafe) — failing to tier gates by reversibility and blast radius

Logging only the final assistant message rather than each tool call with its arguments, model version and prompt/registry version, leaving actions unattributable and non-reconstructable for audit or rollback

Omitting runtime safety limits — no action/cost budget, loop detection or kill switch — and treating the shared tool/prompt registry as static so newly added tools silently expand the capability surface
reference_answer:
The governing principle is that the LLM is not a trust boundary: authorization must be enforced at the tool boundary, and the strictness of every control scales with an action's blast radius and reversibility. The central trade-off is autonomy/velocity vs. blast radius/reversibility, and I default to least autonomy for anything irreversible, loosening gates only as eval evidence accumulates.

(1) Permission & identity model. The agent runs under its own dedicated, scoped service identity, never a human's broad credentials or a single super-token. Each tool is granted least-privilege permissions: read-only SQL hits replicas with a read-only role; Terraform and pod-restart tools get narrowly scoped roles per environment. Registering a tool grants capability, so the registry is itself governed by RBAC, ownership, versioning, and review — a new tool expands the capability surface and must be re-evaluated, not silently trusted. When acting for a user, the agent carries an on-behalf-of identity so its effective permissions are the intersection of the agent's and the requester's.

(2) Risk-tiered human-in-the-loop. Classify actions by reversibility/blast radius. Read-only queries and Slack posts to low-stakes channels auto-execute with logging. Reversible low-risk writes run with logging and rate caps. Irreversible or high-blast actions — Terraform apply, merging to prod, pod restarts — require an explicit human approval gate, and infra tools must plan/dry-run first so a human approves a concrete diff. Uniform gating on everything destroys the value; auto-approving everything is unsafe — hence tiering.

(3) Prompt-injection threat model. Tool outputs and retrieved content are attacker-controllable and may contain instructions; the danger is the "lethal trifecta": access to sensitive data + exposure to untrusted content + ability to take consequential/exfiltrating actions. Mitigations: never let untrusted content directly authorize a privileged call — enforce allowlists and approval at the tool boundary regardless of what the model "decided"; tag data provenance and keep untrusted content out of privileged planning where possible; constrain tool arguments (schemas, parameter allowlists); and treat the model's chosen action as a request, not a grant.

(4) Auditability and runtime controls. Emit an immutable, structured audit record per tool call: triggering user, timestamp, tool + arguments + result, the system-prompt/registry version, model + version, and a trace/correlation id linking the reasoning step to the action — enough to reconstruct and roll back. Add action/cost budgets and loop-detection per session (halt on runaway), plus global and per-tool kill switches / feature flags. Ship in stages: shadow mode, then canary to a few teams with write tools disabled, gated by offline evals and adversarial injection red-teaming before privileged tools are enabled, with a documented rollback plan.
